scene.label: Act 3, Scene 3
scene.title: SCENE III. Another part of the Forest

content.text: Enter Touchstone and Audrey; Jaques at a distance observing them.

lines.text: Come apace, good Audrey. I will fetch up your goats, Audrey. And how, Audrey? Am I the man yet? Doth my simple feature content you?
lines.plainText: Come apace good Audrey I will fetch up your goats Audrey And how Audrey Am I the man yet Doth my simple feature content you

lines.text: Your features, Lord warrant us! What features?
lines.plainText: Your features Lord warrant us What features

lines.text: I am here with thee and thy goats, as the most capricious poet, honest Ovid, was among the Goths.
lines.plainText: I am here with thee and thy goats as the most capricious poet honest Ovid was among the Goths

lines.text: [Aside.] O knowledge ill-inhabited, worse than Jove in a thatched house!
lines.plainText: Aside O knowledge illinhabited worse than Jove in a thatched house

lines.text: When a man's verses cannot be understood, nor a man's good wit seconded with the forward child, understanding, it strikes a man more dead than a great reckoning in a little room. Truly, I would the gods had made thee poetical.
lines.plainText: When a man's verses cannot be understood nor a man's good wit seconded with the forward child understanding it strikes a man more dead than a great reckoning in a little room Truly I would the gods had made thee poetical

lines.text: I do not know what "poetical" is. Is it honest in deed and word? Is it a true thing?
lines.plainText: I do not know what poetical is Is it honest in deed and word Is it a true thing

lines.text: No, truly; for the truest poetry is the most feigning, and lovers are given to poetry, and what they swear in poetry may be said, as lovers, they do feign.
lines.plainText: No truly for the truest poetry is the most feigning and lovers are given to poetry and what they swear in poetry may be said as lovers they do feign

lines.text: Do you wish, then, that the gods had made me poetical?
lines.plainText: Do you wish then that the gods had made me poetical

lines.text: I do, truly, for thou swear'st to me thou art honest. Now if thou wert a poet, I might have some hope thou didst feign.
lines.plainText: I do truly for thou swear'st to me thou art honest Now if thou wert a poet I might have some hope thou didst feign

lines.text: Would you not have me honest?
lines.plainText: Would you not have me honest

lines.text: No, truly, unless thou wert hard-favoured; for honesty coupled to beauty is to have honey a sauce to sugar.
lines.plainText: No truly unless thou wert hardfavoured for honesty coupled to beauty is to have honey a sauce to sugar

lines.text: [Aside.] A material fool!
lines.plainText: Aside A material fool

lines.text: Well, I am not fair, and therefore I pray the gods make me honest.
lines.plainText: Well I am not fair and therefore I pray the gods make me honest

lines.text: Truly, and to cast away honesty upon a foul slut were to put good meat into an unclean dish.
lines.plainText: Truly and to cast away honesty upon a foul slut were to put good meat into an unclean dish

lines.text: I am not a slut, though I thank the gods I am foul.
lines.plainText: I am not a slut though I thank the gods I am foul

lines.text: Well, praised be the gods for thy foulness; sluttishness may come hereafter. But be it as it may be, I will marry thee. And to that end I have been with Sir Oliver Martext, the vicar of the next village, who hath promised to meet me in this place of the forest and to couple us.

lines.text: [Aside.] I would fain see this meeting.
lines.plainText: Aside I would fain see this meeting

lines.text: Well, the gods give us joy!
lines.plainText: Well the gods give us joy

lines.text: Amen. A man may, if he were of a fearful heart, stagger in this attempt, for here we have no temple but the wood, no assembly but horn-beasts. But what though? Courage! As horns are odious, they are necessary. It is said, "Many a man knows no end of his goods." Right. Many a man has good horns and knows no end of them. Well, that is the dowry of his wife; 'tis none of his own getting. Horns? Even so. Poor men alone? No, no, the noblest deer hath them as huge as the rascal. Is the single man therefore blessed? No. As a walled town is more worthier than a village, so is the forehead of a married man more honourable than the bare brow of a bachelor. And by how much defence is better than no skill, by so much is horn more precious than to want.

lines.text: Is there none here to give the woman?
lines.plainText: Is there none here to give the woman

lines.text: I will not take her on gift of any man.
lines.plainText: I will not take her on gift of any man

lines.text: Truly, she must be given, or the marriage is not lawful.
lines.plainText: Truly she must be given or the marriage is not lawful

lines.text: [Coming forward.] Proceed, proceed. I'll give her.
lines.plainText: Coming forward Proceed proceed I'll give her

lines.text: Good even, good Master What-ye-call't, how do you, sir? You are very well met. God 'ild you for your last company. I am very glad to see you. Even a toy in hand here, sir. Nay, pray be covered.
lines.plainText: Good even good Master Whatyecall't how do you sir You are very well met God 'ild you for your last company I am very glad to see you Even a toy in hand here sir Nay pray be covered

lines.text: Will you be married, motley?
lines.plainText: Will you be married motley

lines.text: As the ox hath his bow, sir, the horse his curb, and the falcon her bells, so man hath his desires; and as pigeons bill, so wedlock would be nibbling.
lines.plainText: As the ox hath his bow sir the horse his curb and the falcon her bells so man hath his desires and as pigeons bill so wedlock would be nibbling

lines.text: And will you, being a man of your breeding, be married under a bush like a beggar? Get you to church, and have a good priest that can tell you what marriage is. This fellow will but join you together as they join wainscot; then one of you will prove a shrunk panel, and like green timber, warp, warp.

lines.text: [Aside.] I am not in the mind but I were better to be married of him than of another, for he is not like to marry me well, and not being well married, it will be a good excuse for me hereafter to leave my wife.

lines.text: Go thou with me, and let me counsel thee.
lines.plainText: Go thou with me and let me counsel thee

lines.text: Come, sweet Audrey. We must be married, or we must live in bawdry.
lines.plainText: Come sweet Audrey We must be married or we must live in bawdry

lines.text: Farewell, good Master Oliver. Not
lines.plainText: Farewell good Master Oliver Not

lines.text: O sweet Oliver,
lines.plainText: O sweet Oliver

lines.text: O brave Oliver,
lines.plainText: O brave Oliver

lines.text: Leave me not behind thee.
lines.plainText: Leave me not behind thee

lines.text: But
lines.plainText: But

lines.text: Wind away,—
lines.plainText: Wind away

lines.text: Begone, I say,
lines.plainText: Begone I say

lines.text: I will not to wedding with thee.
lines.plainText: I will not to wedding with thee

lines.text: 'Tis no matter. Ne'er a fantastical knave of them all shall flout me out of my calling.
